analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from permanently replacing workers who strike or join a union.
analysis.headline: The bill was never voted on: it sat in the Senate labor committee until Congress adjourned in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, when workers go on strike, an employer can hire permanent replacements and then legally refuse to give strikers their old jobs back. This bill would change the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act to make that illegal: employers could not grant anyone 'permanent replacement' status, and could not favor strikebreakers over strikers who are working or have offered to return. It would have applied to private-sector workers covered by those laws, including railroad and airline workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Striking workers and union members: they would keep the practical right to stop work without risking their jobs permanently, including railroad and airline workers covered by the Railway Labor Act.

how_it_helps.text: It adds an unfair labor practice making it illegal for an employer to grant 'permanent replacement' status to anyone doing bargaining-unit work during a labor dispute.
It also bars any hiring preference for someone who worked, or was willing to work, as a strikebreaker over an employee who is working or has unconditionally offered to return to work.
It applies the same ban to railroads and airlines under the Railway Labor Act.

analysis.who_pays: Employers covered by the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act: strikes would put more pressure on them because they could no longer permanently replace strikers, raising the cost of resisting union demands.

drawbacks.text: Employers argue that the ability to hire permanent replacements is one of the few lawful tools they have to keep operating during a strike; removing it shifts bargaining leverage heavily toward unions and could lengthen disputes rather than settle them.

The bill was introduced in the final weeks of a Congress with only Democratic sponsorship and was referred to committee; the Senate committee took no recorded action, so there was no hearing record or amendment process to test these trade-offs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For striking workers this is a significant protection: it removes the threat that exercising the right to strike means losing your job for good. The cost falls on employers, who lose a major tool for operating during strikes, and that could stiffen some disputes. The bill never got a hearing or a vote, so those trade-offs were never tested in the legislative process.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late October 2000 and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: It was introduced on October 27, 2000, in the closing weeks of the 106th Congress.
It was referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, where no further action was recorded.
The companion measure is summarized by the Congressional Research Service via S. 3249, an identical or near-identical bill introduced earlier in the same Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who use or could use permanent replacements during strikes are better off: the current-law ability to permanently replace economic strikers was left untouched. Union-side advocates got no change to the law.

for.name: Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

for.name: 15 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Wellstone, Kennedy, Murray, Boxer, Mikulski, Lieberman, Rockefeller, Bingaman, Feingold, Akaka, Sarbanes, Leahy, Dodd, Kerry, and Baucus

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and no committee or floor vote was ever held, so there is no record of how senators would have lined up if it had come to a vote.

industries.note: The bill removes the threat of permanent replacement, which is the main legal risk workers take when they strike. It applies to both private-sector workers under the NLRA and railroad and airline workers under the Railway Labor Act.

industries.industry: Employers covered by the NLRA and the Railway Labor Act
industries.note: They would lose the ability to permanently replace strikers, which is one of the main legal levers they can use against a strike. This raises the cost of a strike for the employer and raises its bargaining power for the union.
